# Economics of Multi-Token-Prediction Speculative Decoding

## 1. The Cost Model

Define the quantities that matter:

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| $T$ | Wall-clock time for one forward pass of the **target** model |
| $C_d$ | Wall-clock time for one forward pass of the **MTP head** (parallel: all $K$ tokens in one shot) |
| $\rho = C_d / T$ | Draft-to-target cost ratio (≈ $P_h / P_t$ in the memory-bound regime, ≈ FLOPs ratio in the compute-bound regime) |
| $K$ | Number of speculative tokens proposed per step |
| $\alpha_j$ | Probability that the $j$-th draft token is accepted, given all prior $j{-}1$ were accepted |
| $B$ | Batch size |
| $\mu$ | Expected tokens emitted per speculative step |

For a **parallel** MTP head (the DeepSeek-style module), the draft cost is a single forward of the head regardless of $K$. For an **autoregressive** head it would be $K \cdot C_d$; I treat the parallel case throughout and note where the distinction matters.

The expected tokens per step (with possibly non-uniform $\alpha_j$):

$$
\mu \;=\; \sum_{m=0}^{K}(m+1)\Bigl[\Bigl(\prod_{j=1}^{m}\alpha_j\Bigr)(1-\alpha_{m+1})\Bigr]
\;+\;(K+1)\prod_{j=1}^{K}\alpha_j
$$

Under the simplifying assumption of a **uniform** rate $\alpha$ at every position this collapses to the geometric-series identity

$$
\mu(\alpha,K) \;=\; \frac{1-\alpha^{K+1}}{1-\alpha}
$$

---

## 2. Speedup as a Function of Regime and Batch

The critical distinction is whether the GPU is **memory-bound** (small $B$, large context: time is dominated by HBM weight streaming) or **compute-bound** (large $B$: time is dominated by FLOPs).

### Memory-bound regime ($B$ small, $L \gg K$)

The extra $K$ positions in the verify pass add negligible FLOPs relative to the weight-reading cost, so the verify step costs $\approx T$ (the same as a normal decode step). The draft head costs $C_d$.

$$
\boxed{S_{\text{mem}} \;=\; \frac{T}{T + C_d}\;\mu \;=\; \frac{\mu}{1+\rho_m}}
$$

where $\rho_m \approx P_h / P_t$ (ratio of parameters that must be streamed from HBM).

### Compute-bound regime ($B$ large)

Now the verify step genuinely processes $K$ new tokens per sequence, so its FLOPs (and hence wall-clock time) scale as $K \cdot T$. The parallel head still costs $C_d$ (one forward, independent of $K$).

$$
\boxed{S_{\text{comp}} \;=\; \frac{K\,T}{K\,T + C_d}\;\mu \;=\; \frac{K\,\mu}{K + \rho_c}}
$$

where $\rho_c \approx \text{FLOPs}_h / \text{FLOPs}_t$ per token.

> **Key asymmetry.** In the memory-bound regime the overhead ratio is $\rho_m$; in the compute-bound regime it is effectively $\rho_c / K$. The $K\times$ verify cost *dilutes* the draft overhead, so the compute-bound regime is actually **easier** to make profitable *if* $\mu$ is large enough. But the absolute throughput ceiling is lower because you are spending $K$ units of target compute per step.

### Numerical illustration ($K=4$, uniform $\alpha$)

| $\alpha$ | $\mu$ | $\rho_m=0.05$ → $S_{\text{mem}}$ | $\rho_c=0.19$ → $S_{\text{comp}}$ |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| 0.70 | 2.57 | **2.45×** | 0.61× |
| 0.50 | 1.94 | **1.84×** ← your 1.8× | 0.46× |
| 0.30 | 1.43 | 1.36× | 0.34× |
| 0.20 | 1.25 | 1.19× | 0.30× |
| 0.10 | 1.11 | 1.06× | 0.27× |
| 0.05 | 1.05 | 1.00× | 0.25× |

The 1.8× you observe corresponds to $\alpha \approx 0.50$ with a light head ($\rho_m \approx 0.05$) in the memory-bound regime. The slowdown appears when $\alpha$ falls below the critical value (next section) or when the batch grows into the compute-bound regime.

---

## 3. When It Cannot Pay Off

Set $S = 1$ and solve for the **critical acceptance rate** $\alpha_c$.

### Memory-bound

$$
\frac{1-\alpha_c^{K+1}}{1-\alpha_c} = 1 + \rho_m
$$

For small $\alpha$ (the interesting regime), $\mu \approx 1 + \alpha$, so

$$
\alpha_c \;\approx\; \rho_m
$$

The head's parameter fraction is the floor: if the head is 15 % of the model's parameters, you need $\alpha > 15\%$ at every position just to break even.

### Compute-bound

$$
\frac{K\,\mu}{K + \rho_c} = 1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mu = 1 + \frac{\rho_c}{K}
$$

Using the geometric approximation $\mu \approx 1/(1-\alpha)$:

$$
\alpha_c \;\approx\; \frac{\rho_c}{K + \rho_c}
$$

For $\rho_c = 0.19$, $K = 4$: $\alpha_c \approx 0.045$. Surprisingly low! But this is the *average* rate. The real killer is **non-uniform decay**: if $\alpha_1 = 0.6$ but $\alpha_4 = 0.15$, the effective $\mu$ is well below the uniform-$\alpha$ value and the product $\prod_{j=1}^4 \alpha_j$ in the boundary term becomes negligible. The speedup can dip below 1 even when the *first* token's acceptance looks fine.

### Summary of "cannot pay off" conditions

1. **$\alpha_j < \rho_m$ for any $j$** (memory-bound): even one weak position drags $\mu$ below $1+\rho_m$.
2. **Head is too heavy**: $P_h / P_t > \alpha_{\min}$ where $\alpha_{\min}$ is the worst-position acceptance rate. A 2-layer transformer head on a 7 B model can have $\rho \sim 0.10$–$0.15$; if the model is uncertain (low-entropy prompts, code with many valid continuations), $\alpha$ can be $< 10\%$.
3. **Compute-bound batch with moderate $\alpha$**: the $K\times$ verify cost means you need $\mu > 1 + \rho_c/K$. For $K=8$ and $\rho_c = 0.2$ you need $\alpha > 2.4\%$ on average—achievable, but the *absolute* throughput is capped at $\mu/(K+\rho_c) \cdot T^{-1}$, which for $\alpha=0.5$ is only $0.24\times$ the memory-bound throughput. You are trading latency for a throughput ceiling that is *below* the no-speculation baseline at the same batch.
4. **Non-uniform acceptance with a long tail**: if $\alpha_1 = 0.7$ but $\alpha_2 = 0.2, \alpha_3 = 0.08, \alpha_4 = 0.03$, then $\mu \approx 1 + 0.7 + 0.14 + 0.011 + \cdots \approx 1.85$, and with $\rho_m = 0.10$ you get $S = 1.85/1.10 = 1.68×$—a speedup, but far below the 2.5× you'd predict from $\alpha_1$ alone. If $\alpha_2$ drops to 0.10, $\mu \approx 1.71$, $S = 1.55×$. The marginal tokens are where the economics break.

---

## 4. The Smallest Predictive Experiment

You want to know, **before writing a single line of MTP-head training code**, whether the head will clear the critical threshold for a *new* target model. The answer is a **linear-probe sweep on hidden states**, which takes minutes and requires no new architecture.

### Protocol (≈ 30 min on a single GPU for a 7 B model)

1. **Collect hidden states.**
   Run the target model (in inference mode, with `output_hidden_states=True`) on **200–500 representative sequences** drawn from the *intended deployment distribution* (code, chat, RAG, whatever the model will actually serve). For each position $i$ in each sequence, save:
   - $h_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ — the last-layer hidden state (or the layer the MTP head will attach to).
   - $t_{i+1}, \ldots, t_{i+K}$ — the $K$ tokens the model actually emits (greedy, or sampled with the same temperature you'll use in production).

   Cost: one forward pass per sequence. For 500 × 512-token sequences on a 7 B model, ≈ 10 min on an A100.

2. **Train a linear probe (the minimal head).**
   Fit a single matrix $W \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times K V}$ (or $K$ separate $d \times V$ matrices) by cross-entropy:

   $$
   \min_W \; -\sum_i \sum_{j=1}^{K} \log\, p\bigl(t_{i+j} \;\big|\; h_i\, W_j\bigr)
   $$

   This is a linear regression in $d$ dimensions; it converges in < 1 min. You get $K$ "predicted tokens" per position.

3. **Measure the *positional* acceptance curve.**
   For each $j = 1,\ldots,K$, compute

   $$
   \hat\alpha_j \;=\; \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \mathbf{1}\bigl[\arg\max\, h_i W_j \;=\; t_{i+j}\;\textbf{and all prior positions matched}\bigr]
   $$

   (i.e., the *consecutive* acceptance rate, which is what the speculative-decoding loop actually uses). Also record the **geometric mean** $\bar\alpha = (\prod_j \hat\alpha_j)^{1/K}$ and the **effective $\mu$** by replaying the accept/reject logic on the probe's predictions.

4. **Plug into the speedup formula.**
   - Determine the regime: for your deployment batch $B_{\text{deploy}}$ and context length $L$, compute the arithmetic-intensity $2P_t B_{\text{deploy}} / (P_t \cdot 2/\text{bytes})$ and compare to the GPU's FLOPS/BW ratio. This tells you memory-bound or compute-bound.
   - Estimate $\rho$: count the parameters (or FLOPs) of the *planned* MTP head and divide by the target's.
   - Compute $S_{\text{mem}}$ or $S_{\text{comp}}$ with the measured $\mu$.

### Why this is the *smallest* sufficient experiment

- It requires **no new architecture, no new training loop, no draft-model training**. Just one inference pass + a linear fit.
- The linear probe is a **lower bound** on any non-linear MTP head's acceptance (a 2-layer MLP can only do better). If the linear probe already clears the threshold, you are *guaranteed* a speedup. If it falls short by a wide margin (e.g., $\hat\alpha_1 < \rho_m$), no reasonable non-linear head will rescue you and you should skip the MTP head entirely or redesign it (lighter, or attached to a different layer).
- It captures the **non-uniform $\alpha_j$** decay, which is the most common reason real deployments see less speedup than the uniform-$\alpha$ formula predicts.
- It is **domain-sensitive**: run it on the actual deployment distribution, not a generic benchmark. A model that is 80 % confident on prose may be 40 % confident on code, and the MTP head's acceptance will track that.

### What to do with the result

| Probe outcome | Decision |
|---|---|
| $\hat\mu > 1 + \rho_m$ **and** $\hat\mu > 1 + \rho_c/K$ | Build the head. Expect speedup in both regimes. |
| $\hat\mu > 1 + \rho_m$ but $\hat\mu < 1 + \rho_c/K$ | Build the head, but **gate it on batch size**: enable for $B \le B^*$ (memory-bound), disable for $B > B^*$ (compute-bound). |
| $\hat\mu < 1 + \rho_m$ | Do **not** build the head. The information in $h_i$ is insufficient. Consider a smaller $K$, a different attachment layer, or a separate small draft model instead. |

### Optional refinement (still cheap)

If the linear probe is borderline, add a **2-layer MLP probe** ($d \to 4d \to KV$, ReLU) trained for 500 steps. This approximates the non-linear MTP head's ceiling. The delta $\alpha_{\text{MLP}} - \alpha_{\text{linear}}$ tells you how much "non-linearity headroom" exists. If the delta is $< 2$ percentage points, the linear result is essentially the truth and you can make your go/no-go call on that.

---

## 5. One-Paragraph Summary

The speedup is $\mu/(1+\rho_m)$ in the memory-bound regime and $K\mu/(K+\rho_c)$ in the compute-bound regime, where $\mu = (1-\alpha^{K+1})/(1-\alpha)$ for a uniform acceptance rate $\alpha$ and $\rho$ is the head's parameter-or-FLOP fraction of the target. Your observed 1.8× corresponds to $\alpha \approx 0.50$ and $\rho_m \approx 0.05$ at small batch. It slows down when $\alpha$ drops below $\rho_m$ (light head) or below $\rho_c/K$ (compute-bound), or when the *positional* acceptance curve decays faster than the geometric model assumes. The single cheapest experiment that disambiguates all of these for a new model is: **run the target on 200–500 domain-representative sequences, save last-layer hidden states, fit a $d \times KV$ linear probe, and measure the consecutive acceptance rate at each of the $K$ positions.** Thirty minutes of GPU time, no new architecture, and a conservative (lower-bound) prediction of the MTP head's economics.

# Classifying Datasets: Master Data vs. Transactional

## Core Hypothesis

Master data is **descriptive, slowly-changing, and referenced**. Transactional data is **event-based, high-volume, append-heavy, and references master data**. The algorithm should score a dataset along several orthogonal axes and combine them into a decision.

---

## 1. Temporal / Change-Pattern Analysis

This is the strongest signal. For each table, compute over a lookback window (e.g., 90 days):

| Metric | Calculation | Master signal | Transactional signal |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Insert-to-Update ratio (IUR)** | `COUNT(inserts) / COUNT(updates)` | High (few updates) | Low or ~1 (constant churn) |
| **Append ratio** | `COUNT(inserts) / (COUNT(inserts)+COUNT(updates)+COUNT(deletes))` | Low | High (>0.8) |
| **Update frequency per row** | `COUNT(DISTINCT updated_at) / COUNT(*)` | ~0 | >0 |
| **Time-of-day entropy of `created_at`** | Shannon entropy of hour-of-day distribution | Low (batch loads) | High (continuous events) |

```
temporal_score = 0.4 * normalize(IUR) 
               + 0.3 * (1 - append_ratio)
               + 0.3 * (1 - update_freq_per_row)
```

---

## 2. Attribute / Column-Type Profiling

Profile every column and classify it:

- **Identifier**: surrogate PK, natural key, FK
- **Descriptor**: name, address, category, status, code
- **Measure**: amount, quantity, price, duration
- **Timestamp**: created_at, event_date, effective_date
- **Geospatial / Hierarchy**: region, org unit, parent_id

Then compute:

```
descriptor_ratio  = count(descriptor cols) / total_cols
measure_ratio     = count(measure cols) / total_cols
fk_ratio          = count(fk cols) / total_cols
timestamp_ratio   = count(timestamp cols) / total_cols
```

- **Master**: high `descriptor_ratio`, low `measure_ratio`, low `fk_ratio`
- **Transactional**: high `measure_ratio`, high `fk_ratio`, ≥1 timestamp

```
attribute_score = descriptor_ratio - measure_ratio - 0.5 * fk_ratio
```

---

## 3. Cardinality & Volume Analysis

For each column, compute **distinct-value ratio** (DVR = `COUNT(DISTINCT col) / COUNT(*)`).

- **Master tables**: a few columns with DVR ≈ 1.0 (keys), many columns with very low DVR (descriptors like `country`, `category`). Overall **low average DVR**.
- **Transactional tables**: at least one high-DVR timestamp or event-ID column; measures have continuous distributions.

```
avg_dvr = mean(DVR across all columns)
max_dvr_gap = max(DVR) - median(DVR)   # spike detection
```

Also track **row growth rate**: `Δrows / Δtime`. Transactional tables grow linearly and fast; master tables grow slowly or plateau.

---

## 4. Referential / Graph Position

If you have metadata (schema catalog, lineage):

- **In-degree** = number of other tables that FK-reference this table
- **Out-degree** = number of FK columns in this table

```
referential_score = in_degree - out_degree
```

- Master → high in-degree, low out-degree (it's the "hub")
- Transactional → low in-degree, high out-degree (it points *at* master)

If lineage isn't available, approximate with **column-name heuristics** (`customer_id`, `product_code` → likely FK) and join-log analysis.

---

## 5. Distributional / Entropy Checks

For each numeric column compute:

- **Skewness & kurtosis** – measures (amounts) are often right-skewed; descriptors encoded as codes are near-uniform or sparse.
- **Shannon entropy** of categorical columns – a `status` column with 3 values has low entropy; a `transaction_id` has very high entropy.

```
avg_categorical_entropy = mean(entropy(col) for categorical cols)
```

Low average entropy → master. High → transactional.

---

## 6. Structural Heuristics (quick signals)

- **Column count**: master tables tend to have more descriptive columns (10–40+); transactional fact tables often 5–15.
- **Presence of effective-dating columns** (`valid_from`, `valid_to`, `as_of_date`) → strong master / SCD signal.
- **Surrogate vs. natural PK**: surrogate keys (`int` auto-increment) lean transactional; natural/business keys lean master.
- **Row count magnitude**: master is typically orders of magnitude smaller than the transactional tables that reference it.

---

## 7. Putting It Together

Combine the sub-scores into a weighted composite:

```
score = w1 * temporal_score        # 0.30
      + w2 * attribute_score       # 0.25
      + w3 * cardinality_score     # 0.15
      + w4 * referential_score     # 0.20
      + w5 * entropy_score         # 0.10
```

Classify:

```
if score >  threshold_high   → MASTER
if score <  threshold_low    → TRANSACTIONAL
else                         → HYBRID / REVIEW  (e.g., slowly-changing dimension with audit trail)
```

Thresholds can be set empirically on a labelled sample, or via a simple **k-means / 1-D GMM** on the score distribution to find the natural split. Once you have ~50–100 labelled tables, you can train a lightweight **logistic regression or gradient-boosted tree** on the feature vector (IUR, append_ratio, descriptor_ratio, fk_ratio, avg_dvr, in_degree, avg_entropy, …) for higher accuracy.

---

## 8. Practical Caveats

- **Hybrids exist**: an `order_items` table is transactional; a `product` table is master; but a `product_price_history` (SCD Type 2) sits in between. The algorithm should allow a third "dimensional / SCD" bucket.
- **Small tables are noisy**: a 200-row master table and a 200-row sample of transactions look similar. Use **rate-based** metrics (per-day, per-row) rather than raw counts.
- **Run it over a time window**, not a snapshot, to capture change patterns.
- **Validate against known business semantics** (column names, data dictionary) as a sanity check; pure statistics can misfire on oddly-named tables.

This gives you a reproducible, explainable classifier that a data-quality team can run across an entire warehouse to flag tables for deeper profiling, lineage mapping, or stewardship assignment.

# Classifying Datasets: Master Data vs. Transactional

Great question — this is one of those problems where you can build a surprisingly robust classifier by combining a handful of structural, statistical, and temporal signals. Here's how I'd approach it.

---

## 1. Structural / Schema Analysis (cheap, do first)

For each table/column, compute:

| Signal | Calculation | Master lean | Transactional lean |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Timestamp columns** | Count of `TIMESTAMP`/`DATE` cols; check if they look like *event* timestamps (high variance, monotonic) vs. *effective* dates (low variance, sparse) | Effective dates, few | Event timestamps, many, high variance |
| **Numeric "measure" columns** | Fraction of columns whose name matches `amount, qty, price, total, revenue, cost…` **and** whose distribution is continuous (low uniqueness ratio) | Low | High |
| **Categorical / code columns** | Fraction of columns with low cardinality relative to row count (e.g., status, type, category) | High | Low |
| **FK fan-out** | Count of FKs *out* of this table to other tables | Low (self-contained reference) | High (references many master tables) |
| **FK fan-in** | Count of other tables that reference *this* table | **High** (many tables point at it) | Low |

> **Quick heuristic score:** `S_struct = w1·fan_in − w2·fan_out − w3·measure_frac + w4·categorical_frac`
> Positive → master, negative → transactional.

---

## 2. Change-Log / Audit Analysis (the strongest signal)

If you have audit logs, CDC streams, or partitioned snapshots, compute per-table over a rolling window (e.g., 30 days):

- **Insert rate**  `R_ins = Δrows_inserted / Δt`
- **Update rate**  `R_upd = Δrows_updated  / Δt`
- **Delete rate**  `R_del = Δrows_deleted  / Δt`
- **Update-to-Insert ratio**  `ρ = R_upd / R_ins`

| Pattern | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| `R_ins` high & steady, `R_upd ≈ 0`, `R_del ≈ 0` | **Transactional** (append-only events) |
| `R_ins` low, `R_upd` non-zero, `R_del` rare | **Master** (records created once, occasionally corrected) |
| `ρ > 0.1` sustained | Strong master signal |

Also look at **volume growth**: fit a linear regression on row-count snapshots. Transactional tables grow near-linearly with time; master tables grow sub-linearly (log or square-root).

---

## 3. Temporal Distribution of Records

For each row, extract its "birth" timestamp (created / effective date).

- **Inter-arrival time** between consecutive record births (sorted):
  - Transactional → small, roughly constant inter-arrival (Poisson-like)
  - Master → large, irregular gaps
- **Coefficient of variation** of inter-arrival times: low → transactional.
- **Kurtosis / skew** of the birth-date histogram: transactional is flat/uniform; master is bursty (onboarding events, system migrations).

---

## 4. Cardinality & Entropy Profile

For every column `c` with `n` rows and `k` distinct values:

```
uniqueness(c) = k / n
entropy(c)    = −Σ p_i log₂(p_i)   over the k distinct values
```

- Master tables: many columns with **mid-range uniqueness** (0.1–0.9) and **low entropy** (categorical attributes like country, product category).
- Transactional tables: at least one **near-unique surrogate key** (uniqueness ≈ 1) plus columns with **very high entropy** (continuous amounts, timestamps).

Aggregate: `S_entropy = mean(entropy)` and `S_uniq = mean(uniqueness)` across columns.

---

## 5. Referential / Graph Centrality (if you have a metadata graph)

Build a directed graph: edge A→B means "A has an FK to B."

- **In-degree** (how many tables reference this one) → high for master.
- **Out-degree** (how many tables this one references) → high for transactional.
- **Betweenness centrality**: master tables sit on many paths.

---

## 6. Putting It Together – Scoring & Decision

Combine the sub-scores with a weighted logistic model (or even a simple thresholded sum to start):

```
score = w_struct·S_struct
      + w_chg·  f(ρ, R_ins, R_upd, growth_slope)
      + w_temp· f(inter-arrival CV, histogram flatness)
      + w_ent·  f(mean entropy, uniqueness profile)
      + w_ref·  f(in-degree, out-degree)

label = "MASTER"      if score >  τ_high
        "TRANSACTIONAL" if score <  τ_low
        "AMBIGUOUS"   otherwise  → route to human review
```

- Start with **equal weights**, then calibrate `w_i` and thresholds `τ` on a hand-labelled sample (even 50–100 tables) using a simple grid search or logistic regression.
- Keep the `AMBIGUOUS` bucket — reference/lookup tables, slowly-changing-dimension tables, and configuration tables will live in the middle and are legitimately hard to bin.

---

## 7. Practical Caveats I'd Flag

- **Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD Type 2)** look like master data in schema but have transactional-like insert rates. Detect by checking for `valid_from / valid_to` pairs and near-zero update rates.
- **Log/event tables** are transactional but have no FKs at all — the fan-in/fan-out signal goes silent. Rely on temporal + change-log signals there.
- **Dimensional / warehouse tables** (star-schema facts) are transactional; **conformed dimensions** are master. The FK fan-in/out signal handles this well.
- Always run the classifier **per table**, not per database, and re-score periodically (a table's character can drift).

---

The change-log / audit signals (§2) and the FK fan-in/out (§1, §5) will give you ~80 % of the lift on their own. The temporal and entropy features (§3, §4) are the tie-breakers for the ambiguous middle. If you don't have audit logs, the structural + cardinality signals alone still work, just with a wider ambiguous band.

# Design Document: Weekly Fail-Fast Funnel for Open-Weight Model Releases

## 1. Purpose and Constraints

Each week, new open-weight model releases (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma, etc.) appear. We evaluate them on **one machine** with a fixed weekly time budget. The goal is to spend the bulk of that budget on the small number of candidates that actually clear the bar, while eliminating the rest in seconds or minutes.

Hard constraints:

- **One machine, one week.** Total GPU-hours available is fixed (e.g., 40 h on a single A100-80G). Every stage must be budgeted against that.
- **Fail-fast.** A candidate that fails at stage *k* never reaches stage *k+1*.
- **Reproducible.** Every score is a function of (weights, prompt, sampling params, eval harness version). Same inputs → same outputs.

---

## 2. The Stages

Stages are ordered strictly by cost. Each stage has a single question: *"Is there a cheap, mechanical test that can eliminate this candidate?"* If yes, run it. If the candidate passes, promote it.

| Stage | Name | Budget | Cheapest disqualifying test | Promote-on evidence |
|-------|------|--------|----------------------------|---------------------|
| 0 | Triage | < 1 min, no GPU | Weights don't download; license incompatible with our use; architecture unsupported by our inference stack; parameter count / context length outside our hardware envelope | Metadata matches the requirements checklist |
| 1 | Smoke | < 5 min GPU | Model fails to load; crashes on first forward pass; outputs are token soup or repeats | 10 fixed prompts produce coherent, on-topic text (checked by a small judge model or exact-match on expected substrings) |
| 2 | Core benchmark | 15–40 min GPU | Score on a **fixed 500-question set** (MMLU-style MCQ + GSM8K-style math + a short coding set) falls below a **pre-registered floor** (e.g., 10 pts below our current production model) | Meets the floor on every sub-task |
| 3 | Application eval | 1–4 h GPU | Fails on **our own task set** (the prompts we actually serve in production, scored by a judge LLM against a pre-written rubric) below the application bar | ≥ 90 % of rubric items pass; no single task category below 70 % |
| 4 | Stress & safety | 2–6 h GPU | Adversarial / jailbreak prompts produce harmful output; long-context (> 32k) generation degrades past a threshold; repeated sampling shows variance that violates a stability band | Passes all red-team probes; context degradation within tolerance |
| 5 | Shadow deploy | 1–3 days wall-clock | Live shadow traffic shows latency regression > 20 % or quality regression on a held-out production slice | Meets SLOs; quality ≥ current model on the slice |

A candidate that reaches stage 5 is a **promotion candidate** for the fleet. Everything else is logged and retired.

### Why this ordering

The expensive tests (stage 3–5) are only meaningful if the model is *competent at all*. Stage 2's 500-question set is the single highest-leverage filter: it distinguishes "broken / toy" from "actually usable" at roughly 1 % of the cost of a full application eval. Most weekly releases die here or earlier.

---

## 3. What "Evidence Promotes a Candidate" Means Concretely

Promotion is **threshold-based, not vibes-based**. Each stage writes a structured record:

```json
{
  "model_id": "org/model-v2-70b",
  "stage": 2,
  "timestamp": "2025-07-14T09:32:00Z",
  "harness_version": "evalkit-3.2.1",
  "scores": {"mmlu": 78.4, "gsm8k": 61.0, "coding": 55.2},
  "floor":   {"mmlu": 72, "gsm8k": 55, "coding": 50},
  "verdict": "PROMOTE",
  "artifacts": ["runs/2025-07-14/model-v2-70b/stage2/"]
}
```

A candidate is promoted only when **every** sub-threshold in the record is met. There is no "it's close enough, let's give it a shot at stage 3." The thresholds are set once per quarter and versioned.

---

## 4. Avoiding Re-Testing What Is Already Known

This is the single biggest source of wasted GPU-hours in a weekly loop, because model families iterate fast (Llama 3.1 → 3.2 → 4) and a lot of the evaluation is redundant.

### 4.1 Content-addressed eval cache

Every evaluation run is keyed by a hash of:

```
key = sha256(
    model_weights_blob_id,   # from the HF repo, not the model name
    prompt_set_version,
    sampling_params,         # temperature, top_p, max_tokens
    harness_version,
    judge_model_id           # if a judge LLM is used
)
```

Before any stage runs, the pipeline checks a persistent SQLite/Postgres table (`eval_results`). If the key exists, the cached score is reused and the stage is skipped. This means:

- Re-running the weekly scan after a crash costs zero GPU.
- If a model is re-released with identical weights (renamed repo), it's a cache hit.

### 4.2 Delta evaluation for fine-tunes and distills

When a new release shares a base checkpoint (e.g., "Qwen3-32B-Instruct" is a fine-tune of "Qwen3-32B"), the base's stage-2 scores are already cached. The pipeline runs only the **delta prompts**: the subset of the eval set on which the fine-tune is expected to differ (instruction-following, formatting, refusal behaviour). This typically cuts stage-2 time by 60–80 %.

The delta set is defined per family and versioned alongside the full set.

### 4.3 Family-level short-circuits

If a model family has been evaluated three consecutive weeks and the new release is a "refresh" (same architecture, same size, incremental training), stage 1 and stage 2 use a **reduced prompt set** (100 questions instead of 500) unless the release notes claim a major training change. The full set is re-run only when the reduced set shows a > 3-point swing.

### 4.4 What is never cached

- Stage 4 (safety / adversarial) is **never** served from cache, because the adversarial set is rotated weekly and because a model that was safe last week can regress with a new fine-tune.
- Stage 5 (shadow deploy) is never cached by definition.

---

## 5. Keeping the Process Honest When a Favourite Is Failing

This is the hardest part and the part that silently breaks most eval pipelines. The risk: a model you've invested in, championed, or built your roadmap around fails stage 3. The natural response is to "try one more thing" — a different temperature, a different prompt, a second run "to confirm." Each rescue attempt is a confirmation-bias loop that burns the week's budget and delays the real decision.

### 5.1 Pre-register the criteria

Thresholds, prompt sets, judge rubrics, and sampling parameters are written into a **versioned config file** (`eval_config_2025Q3.yaml`) **before** the weekly scan begins. The pipeline reads that file; it does not accept ad-hoc overrides at run time. If you want to change a threshold, you do it for next week's scan and the change is logged with a reason.

### 5.2 Mechanical verdicts, no human in the loop at stages 0–4

Stages 0–4 are fully automated. The pipeline emits `PROMOTE` or `RETIRE` from the config. A human does not "look at the outputs and decide it's actually fine." If a human disagrees with a verdict, they file an **override ticket** that is logged, attributed, and reviewed at the weekly retro. The override does not re-run the eval with tweaked parameters; it triggers a *new* eval with a *new*, pre-registered config.

### 5.3 No re-run rescues

If a candidate fails stage 2, it is retired. There is no "run it again with temperature 0.3 instead of 0.7." The sampling parameters are part of the cache key and the config. If you believe the parameters are wrong, you change the config for next week and re-evaluate **all** candidates under the new parameters.

### 5.4 The "favourite" log

Every override, every threshold change, every "let me just look at these outputs" is written to an append-only log with the person's name and timestamp. At the weekly retro, the log is reviewed. If the same person has overridden three favourites in a row, that pattern is visible and can be discussed. The log is not punitive; it is a calibration instrument.

### 5.5 Separate the person who sets criteria from the person who runs the scan

If possible, the eval config (thresholds, prompt sets, rubrics) is owned by one person or team, and the weekly execution is owned by another. This is the cheapest structural guard against the person who loves the model also tuning the bar to let it through. On a one-machine shop this may be the same person wearing two hats on different days; the key is that the config is frozen before the scan and the scan is run mechanically.

### 5.6 A "control" candidate every week

Each weekly scan includes one **known-good** model (your current production model) and one **known-bad** model (a deliberately weak or broken checkpoint). These run through the full funnel. If the known-good fails or the known-bad passes, the harness itself is broken and **no verdicts that week are trusted**. This catches silent regressions in the eval code, the judge model, or the inference stack that would otherwise be mistaken for model quality.

---

## 6. Weekly Operating Cadence

| Day | Activity |
|-----|----------|
| Mon AM | Scan Hugging Face / release feeds. Populate the candidate list. Run stage 0 (triage) on everything. |
| Mon PM | Stage 1 (smoke) on survivors. Typically 3–8 candidates remain. |
| Tue | Stage 2 (core benchmark) on survivors. Typically 1–3 remain. |
| Wed–Thu | Stage 3 (application eval) on survivors. |
| Fri AM | Stage 4 (stress & safety) on any candidate that passed stage 3. |
| Fri PM | If a candidate passed stage 4, queue stage 5 (shadow deploy) for the following week. Write the weekly report: what was tested, what passed, what failed, any overrides. |

If no candidate reaches stage 4, the week ends with a short "no promotion" report. That is a valid and common outcome. The funnel's job is to make "nothing new is good enough" a fast, cheap conclusion rather than a three-day slog.

---

## 7. Artefacts and Tooling

- **`evalkit`** – the harness. A Python package that loads a model, runs a prompt set, scores outputs, and writes the structured record. Versioned. Pinned in the config.
- **`eval_results` DB** – persistent store of every run, keyed as in §4.1. Survives machine reboots; lives on a small SSD or network share.
- **`eval_config_YYYYQn.yaml`** – thresholds, prompt-set versions, sampling params, judge model ID. One file per quarter, reviewed at quarter boundaries.
- **`override_log.md`** – append-only, human-written, reviewed weekly.
- **Weekly report** – auto-generated from the DB: table of candidates × stages × verdicts, with links to raw run directories.

---

## 8. Open Questions / Future Work

- **Judge model drift.** The LLM judge used in stages 3–4 is itself a model that changes. When the judge is updated, all downstream scores shift. Mitigation: pin the judge version in the config; re-baseline all thresholds when the judge changes.
- **Multi-GPU or multi-machine scaling.** The design assumes one box. If a second machine is added, stages 3–4 can be parallelised across candidates, but the funnel ordering and caching keys stay the same.
- **Continuous vs. weekly.** If release cadence exceeds weekly, the triage stage (stage 0) can run daily and the rest of the funnel runs weekly on the accumulated survivors. The cache makes this cheap.

---

*Document owner: [eval team]. Review cadence: quarterly, aligned to config version bumps.*

# Design Document: Fail-Fast Funnel for Weekly Open-Weight Model Evaluation

## 1. Purpose and Constraints

This document specifies a staged evaluation pipeline that screens every new open-weight model release each week and promotes only the survivors to progressively more expensive testing. The goal is to spend the week's compute on the models that matter and to reject the rest within minutes.

**Hard constraints**

| Constraint | Implication |
|---|---|
| One machine | Total GPU-hours per week is fixed (call it *B*). Every stage must have a hard budget cap. |
| Weekly cadence | The funnel must complete for all candidates within one calendar week, leaving time for the expensive stages. |
| Open-weight releases | Checkpoints vary from ~1 B to 70 B+ parameters; context lengths, tokenizers, and architectures differ. |
| Fail-fast ordering | Stages are ordered strictly by expected cost. A candidate that fails at stage *k* never pays for stage *k+1*. |

## 2. The Funnel: Stages, Cheapest Disqualifier, Promotion Evidence

Each stage has three properties: a **budget cap** (max compute before the stage must conclude), a **disqualifying test** (the single cheapest check that can reject), and a **promotion criterion** (the evidence required to advance).

### Stage 0 — Triage (budget: < 1 min, no model load)

Read the model card, `config.json`, and release metadata. Do **not** download weights yet.

- **Cheapest disqualifier:** Any of —
  - License incompatible with your use (e.g., non-commercial-only when you need commercial).
  - Parameter count or context length makes the model impossible to serve on your hardware at the precision you require.
  - Release is structurally broken: missing tokenizer files, no `model.safetensors`, architecture string your runtime doesn't support.
- **Promotion evidence:** A one-line triage record in the ledger (see §4): model name, version, param count, license, architecture, context length, and a go/no-go flag with the rule that fired.

### Stage 1 — Load-and-Smoke (budget: < 5 min, weights on disk)

Download the checkpoint (or pull from a local mirror), load it, and run a fixed set of **5 prompts** through a single forward pass.

- **Cheapest disqualifier:** Any of —
  - Load failure (corrupt weights, shape mismatch, OOM at the minimum viable precision).
  - Degenerate output on ≥ 3 of 5 prompts: repeated token loops, all-`<pad>` output, single-character repetition, or output that is not in the tokenizer's vocabulary.
- **Promotion evidence:** All 5 prompts produce syntactically plausible text. Record the 5 outputs verbatim in the ledger.

### Stage 2 — Cheap Capability Probe (budget: < 30 min)

Run a **fixed 200-example probe set** covering the capability axes you actually care about (e.g., instruction following, extraction, summarisation, code, multilingual). The set is versioned and immutable within a week.

- **Cheapest disqualifier:** Score below a **floor threshold** (start at 30 % exact-match / pass-rate; tune after 4–6 weeks of data). This catches models that load fine but are effectively useless for your workload.
- **Promotion evidence:** Score ≥ floor. Record the per-axis breakdown, not just the aggregate, so Stage 3 can target weak axes.

### Stage 3 — Targeted Evaluation (budget: < 4 h)

Run the **full evaluation suite** you use for operational decisions, but on a **subset** (e.g., 25 % of each benchmark, seeded deterministically). Compare against the **incumbent** (the model currently in production or the best model from the previous week's funnel).

- **Cheapest disqualifier:** Regression below the incumbent on **two or more** of your top-3 operational metrics, or a > 10-point drop on any single metric.
- **Promotion evidence:** No regression on any top-3 metric AND an improvement of ≥ 2 points on at least one. Record the full per-task scorecard.

### Stage 4 — Full Evaluation and Promotion Decision (budget: remainder of the week)

Run the complete benchmark suite at full sample size, with **3 seeds** for variance estimation. Produce a final scorecard and a written promotion/rejection rationale.

- **Disqualifier:** Fails to beat the incumbent on the composite score after variance correction, or shows high variance (std > 5 points) that makes the improvement claim unreliable.
- **Promotion evidence:** A signed-off scorecard in the ledger with the composite score, per-axis deltas vs. incumbent, and a one-paragraph rationale. Only models reaching here are candidates for a production swap.

> **Budget invariant:** The sum of the caps for Stages 0–3 must be ≤ 60 % of *B*, so that even if every candidate survives to Stage 4 you still have compute left. If a week's releases exceed the Stage 2 budget, you triage by recency and community signal and explicitly log which models were skipped and why.

## 3. The Fixed Probe and Evaluation Sets

- The Stage 2 probe set (200 examples) and the Stage 3/4 evaluation suite are **versioned artefacts** (e.g., `probe-v7.jsonl`, `eval-suite-v12/`).
- Changing a set increments its version. You never silently edit prompts in place.
- A model is always scored against a specific set version. This is what makes results comparable across weeks (see §4).

## 4. Avoiding Re-Testing What Is Already Known

The core mechanism is a **content-addressed result ledger** (a local SQLite or Parquet file is sufficient on one machine).

### 4.1 Result keys

Every evaluation result is keyed by the tuple:

```
(model_fingerprint, set_version, prompt_id, precision, seed)
```

- **model_fingerprint:** SHA-256 of the weight files (or, for speed, a hash of the checkpoint's git commit / Hugging Face revision). Never use the model's display name as the key — names get reused and forked.
- **set_version:** the version string of the probe or eval set.
- **prompt_id / seed:** identifies the individual example and random seed.

### 4.2 Lookup before run

Before any stage executes, query the ledger. If a result exists for the exact key, **skip the computation** and reuse the stored score. This handles:

- **Re-releases of the same checkpoint** (same weights, new name).
- **Partial re-runs** after a crash: only the missing `(prompt_id, seed)` cells are computed.
- **Set-version changes:** bumping the set version invalidates old results for that set but preserves results for other sets.

### 4.3 Family-level memoisation

When a model family releases v2 of v1 (e.g., "Llama-3-8B" → "Llama-3.1-8B"), you already know v1's per-axis profile. The ledger stores a **family profile**: the per-axis scores for every prior version. Stage 3 can then run only the axes where v1 was weak or where the release notes claim improvement, rather than re-running the full suite. Log the assumption ("reusing v1 scores for axes X, Y, Z; re-testing axes A, B") in the ledger.

### 4.4 Structural memoisation

If the architecture, tokenizer, and context length are byte-identical to a previously tested model (same `config.json` hash), skip Stage 1 entirely. Only the weights changed; the structural smoke test is redundant.

## 5. Keeping the Process Honest When a Favourite Is Failing

This is the highest-risk part of the pipeline, because the person running the funnel has usually already formed an opinion about which model "should" win. The design mitigates this with four mechanisms.

### 5.1 Pre-registration of the protocol

Before any candidate's results are visible, the evaluation protocol for the week is written into the ledger: which set versions, which thresholds, which metrics count toward the composite score, and the exact pass/fail rules. **The protocol is immutable once the week's candidates are known.** If you discover mid-week that a metric is noisy or a prompt is ambiguous, you fix it for next week's version, not this week's run.

### 5.2 Mechanical gates, not human gates

Stages 0–3 are **automated scripts** that read the ledger, run the tests, compare against the threshold, and write a pass/fail flag. The human does not see the score before the flag is written. The only human judgment point is Stage 4, and even there the composite score is computed by the script; the human writes a rationale but cannot alter the number.

If you override a mechanical fail (e.g., "the probe set has a known bad prompt, so I'm promoting despite the floor miss"), the override is logged as an explicit exception with a reason code. **Track the override rate.** If it exceeds ~10 % of candidates over 8 weeks, the thresholds or the probe set are miscalibrated and need fixing, not the individual judgment.

### 5.3 Blinding

The Stage 0–2 scripts do not print the model's display name, author, or community hype context to the terminal. They print the fingerprint and the score. You see the name only at Stage 4, after the scorecard is locked. This is cheap to implement (the script reads a config that maps fingerprint → display name, and suppresses the name in early-stage output) and it removes the most common source of motivated reasoning: "this is the model everyone is excited about, so let me give it a second chance."

### 5.4 The incumbent is the bar, not the favourite

The Stage 3–4 comparison is always **candidate vs. incumbent**, not candidate vs. "good enough." The incumbent is the model that passed the funnel last week (or the production model). If your favourite is the incumbent and a new model is failing, the new model fails — the favourite's status doesn't lower the bar. Conversely, if the incumbent is failing and a new model passes, the incumbent is demoted. The funnel has no loyalty.

### 5.5 Audit trail

Every week, the ledger contains a complete, append-only log: for each candidate, every stage, the input key, the computed score, the threshold, the flag, and (if overridden) the override reason. At the end of each quarter, review the log for patterns: are overrides clustering on one model family? Are thresholds being "adjusted" the week after a favourite fails? The log makes these patterns visible in a way that memory does not.

## 6. Weekly Operating Procedure (Summary)

1. **Monday, 09:00 — Triage batch.** Collect the week's new releases. Run Stage 0 for each. Log go/no-go.
2. **Monday, 10:00 — Smoke batch.** Stage 1 for all Stage-0 survivors. Log pass/fail.
3. **Monday–Tuesday — Probe batch.** Stage 2 for all Stage-1 survivors. Log per-axis scores.
4. **Wednesday — Targeted eval.** Stage 3 for all Stage-2 survivors. Log scorecards vs. incumbent.
5. **Thursday — Full eval.** Stage 4 for all Stage-3 survivors. Write rationales.
6. **Friday — Decision and ledger close.** Promote or reject. Write the week's summary. Bump set versions if any were flagged. Update the family profiles.

## 7. Tuning and Maintenance

- **Thresholds are empirical.** After 6–8 weeks of ledger data, recalibrate the Stage 2 floor and Stage 3 regression thresholds against the distribution of scores you actually see. The initial values above are starting points.
- **Probe set refresh.** Every 8–12 weeks, retire the oldest 20 % of probe examples and add new ones to prevent overfitting the model to the test. Increment the set version.
- **Budget review.** If a particular stage is consuming more than its cap regularly, either the cap is wrong or the stage's test is too expensive. Fix one, not both, and log the change.
- **Single-machine failure mode.** If the machine is down for more than a day, the week's funnel is incomplete. Log the gap explicitly rather than backfilling with a partial run that looks like a full one.

---

*The entire system is one machine, one ledger, one set of scripts, and one rule: the cheapest test that can say "no" gets to say "no" first, and the person running it is not allowed to argue with it.*

# AI Triage for Radiology: Architecture, Training, and PACS Deployment

## 1. Problem Framing

"Triage" in radiology means **prioritizing and routing studies**, not diagnosis. Concretely, the system answers:

- **Urgency scoring**: Is this a 10-minute emergency (massive PE, pneumothorax, fracture) or a 2-day routine read?
- **Routing**: Send to the right subspecialty (neuroradiology, musculoskeletal, cardiothoracic).
- **Findings flagging**: Surface candidate findings (nodule, effusion, fracture) as bounding boxes or whole-image attention maps so the radiologist reviews the right region first.

This is a **multi-task classification + detection** problem, not a single binary classifier.

---

## 2. Model Architecture

### 2A. Backbone: Vision Transformer (ViT) or ConvNeXt

For 2D CT/MR slices, a **ViT-L/16** or **ConvNeXt-XL** backbone is the current strong default.

```
Input: 224×224 or 384×384 pixel patch (DICOM slice, resampled to 1mm isotropic if 3D)
  → Patch embedding (16×16 patches)
  → 24 transformer layers, 1024-dim, 16 heads
  → [CLS] token → Urgency head (7-class ordinal regression)
  → Per-patch tokens → Detection head (DETR-style, 92 COCO-style classes)
```

**Why ViT over ResNet-50 here:**
- Handles multi-scale pathology (a 3mm pulmonary nodule and a 12cm mass in the same volume) better with global attention.
- Pretrained weights (MAE, DINOv2) transfer well to medical imaging when fine-tuned with a **linear probing → full fine-tune** schedule.

If your data is 3D (CT volumes), use a **3D ViT** (e.g., Swin-3D or a 3D ConvNeXt) operating on 128³ patches, or a **2D-slice ensemble** (read every Nth slice, aggregate with a small GRU/attention pooler) if GPU memory is constrained.

### 2B. Multi-Task Heads

```python
class TriageModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, backbone, num_urgency=7, num_findings=92):
        self.backbone = backbone          # ViT-L/16, returns [CLS] + patch tokens
        self.urgency_head = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(1024, 512), nn.GELU(), nn.Dropout(0.3),
            nn.Linear(512, 7)             # ordinal: routine → stat
        )
        self.finding_head = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(1024, 512), nn.GELU(),
            nn.Linear(512, num_findings)  # multi-label sigmoid
        )
        self.det_head = DETRDecoder(      # optional: bounding boxes
            num_queries=100, num_classes=num_findings
        )
```

**Urgency as ordinal regression**, not 7 independent classes. Use **CORAL loss** (Cao et al. 2020) so misclassifying "routine" as "urgent" costs less than "massive PE" as "routine."

### 2C. Modality Handling

- **X-ray / CT / MRI / US** share the backbone but have **modality-specific adapter layers** (LoRA-style low-rank adapters on the transformer attention, ~1% of params) so you don't retrain everything per modality.
- DICOM pixel data must go through a **modality-aware normalization**: window/level per modality (lung, mediastinum, bone, brain windows for CT; no windowing for X-ray; N4 bias correction + z-score for MRI).

---

## 3. Training Pipeline

### 3A. Data

- **Source**: Anonymized DICOM studies from your own PACS (with IRB/ethics approval) + public datasets (NIH ChestXray14, RSNA, CT-RATE, MedNIST) for pretraining.
- **Labels**: Urgency scores from radiologist reports (NER-extract "STAT," "urgent," "routine" from structured HL7 ORU reports). Finding labels from structured report fields or manual annotation.
- **Scale**: Aim for ≥50k studies for the backbone, ≥10k per urgency class. Class imbalance is severe (95%+ are routine) → use **focal loss** and **class-balanced sampling**.

### 3B. Training Loop

```
Phase 1 (pretrain, 2-4 weeks on 8×A100):
  MAE / DINOv2 self-supervised on 1M unlabeled DICOM slices
  → modality-specific adapters

Phase 2 (supervised fine-tune, 1-2 weeks):
  Full backbone + heads, AdamW, lr=1e-4 → 1e-6 cosine schedule
  3D augmentation: random rotation ±15°, elastic deform, intensity jitter
  2D augmentation: flip, rotation, CutMix
  Loss: CORAL(urgency) + 0.5 * BCEWithLogits(findings) + 1.0 * DETR loss

Phase 3 (calibration):
  Temperature scaling on a held-out validation set
  → calibrated probability outputs (critical for clinical trust)
```

### 3C. Validation

- **Patient-level split** (not study-level) to avoid leakage.
- Report **sensitivity at fixed specificity** (e.g., "catch 95% of STATs at 90% specificity") rather than AUC alone. Radiologists care about missed emergencies, not aggregate discrimination.
- Slice by modality, body part, and urgency class.

---

## 4. PACS Deployment

This is where most projects die. Be specific.

### 4A. DICOM Network Architecture

```
┌──────────────┐    DICOM C-MOVE/C-STORE     ┌──────────────────┐
│  Modalities  │ ──────────────────────────► │     PACS        │
│ (CT, MR, US) │   (DICOM 3.0, port 104)    │ (Orthanc /      │
└──────────────┘                             │  dcm4chee /     │
                                              │  AWS HealthImaging)
                                              └───────┬────────┘
                                                      │
                                          DICOMweb (QIDO-RS, WADO-RS)
                                                      │
                                              ┌───────▼────────┐
                                              │  Triage Service │
                                              │  (FastAPI +    │
                                              │   PyTorch)     │
                                              └───────┬────────┘
                                                      │
                                          HL7 FHIR (Observation,
                                          DiagnosticReport)
                                                      │
                                              ┌───────▼────────┐
                                              │  RIS / Worklist │
                                              │  (prioritized)  │
                                              └────────────────┘
```

### 4B. PACS Choice

| PACS | Why |
|---|---|
| **Orthanc** (self-hosted) | Lightweight, DICOMweb native, Python plugin API, great for dev/test. Not for production volume. |
| **dcm4chee** (self-hosted) | DICOM 3.0 fully compliant, handles C-STORE/C-FIND at scale, DICOMweb built-in. Best open-source production choice. |
| **AWS HealthImaging Archive** | Managed, DICOMweb + FHIR native, scales to millions of studies. Avoids running your own PACS ops. |
| **Existing hospital PACS** (GE, Philips, Agfa) | Integrate via DICOM C-MOVE or DICOMweb if the vendor supports it. Check DICOM conformance statements. |

### 4C. The Triage Service (DICOMweb → Model → FHIR)

```python
# FastAPI service, deployed as a container
@app.post("/triage/{study_uid}")
async def triage_study(study_uid: str):
    # 1. Retrieve DICOM objects via DICOMweb WADO-RS
    #    GET /studies/{study_uid}/series/{series_uid}/instances
    #    → retrieve DICOM bytes, parse with pydicom
    dicom_objects = fetch_dicomweb(pacs_url, study_uid)

    # 2. Preprocess: resample to 1mm iso, apply modality windowing
    tensors = preprocess(dicom_objects)  # → list of 2D or 3D tensors

    # 3. Inference (batch all slices, or 3D volume)
    urgency, findings, boxes = model(tensors)

    # 4. Write back as FHIR resources
    fhir_observations = to_fhir(urgency, findings, boxes)
    post_fhir_bundle(ris_fhir_url, fhir_observations)

    # 5. Update the study's priority in the RIS worklist
    #    (HL7 ORU^R01 or FHIR DiagnosticReport.status)
    update_worklist_priority(study_uid, urgency_class)

    return {"urgency": urgency, "findings": findings}
```

### 4D. Triggering the Pipeline

- **DICOM C-STORE notification**: PACS fires a callback (HL7 ADT/ORM or DICOM DIMSE C-STORE event) when a study arrives. The triage service subscribes and pulls the study via DICOMweb.
- **Polling fallback**: If the PACS doesn't support push notifications, poll QIDO-RS every 10-30s for new studies. Ugly but works.

### 4E. GPU Sizing

- ViT-L/16 on 2D slices: ~4GB VRAM per study. An **A10 (24GB)** or **T4 (16GB)** handles ~3-4 studies in parallel.
- 3D CT volumes: ~12-16GB. Use an **A100 40GB** or **L40S**.
- For a single-center deployment (500-2000 studies/day), **one A100** with a queue (Redis + Celery or a simple asyncio queue) is sufficient. Latency target: **< 30s per study** for triage scoring.

### 4F. Serving the Model

- **TorchServe** or **Triton Inference Server** for the PyTorch model.
- Put a **DICOM preprocessing worker** (pydicom + numpy) in front — it's CPU-bound and shouldn't block GPU inference.
- Run the whole thing in **Kubernetes** (or a single Docker Compose stack for one site):
  - `triage-api` (FastAPI, 2 replicas)
  - `triage-worker` (GPU pod, 1-2 replicas)
  - `redis` (job queue)
  - `orthanc` or connect to existing PACS

---

## 5. Regulatory & Clinical Integration

- **FDA / CE marking**: In the US, this is a **Class II SaMD** (510(k) pathway). You need a predicate device, a well-defined intended use ("prioritization of studies"), and a clinical validation study. The AI doesn't diagnose — it prioritizes — which is a more tractable regulatory path.
- **HIPAA / GDPR**: DICOM de-identification (remove PHI tags per DICOM PS3.15), BAA with cloud PACS provider, audit logging of every inference.
- **Integration with the radiologist's workflow**: The output should appear as **overlays in the existing PACS viewer** (e.g., OHIF, which supports DICOMweb and can render FHIR annotations) or as a **worklist reorder** in the RIS. Don't build a separate viewer.
- **Human-in-the-loop**: The AI scores urgency; a radiologist confirms. Log every disagreement for model monitoring and retraining.

---

## 6. Monitoring & Iteration

- Track **urgency calibration drift** weekly (reliability diagrams on the last 500 studies).
- Alert if sensitivity for STAT-class drops below threshold.
- Collect radiologist corrections (click to accept/reject a finding flag) → feed into a **semi-supervised or active-learning** retraining loop quarterly.

---

**TL;DR stack**: ViT-L/16 backbone with modality adapters + CORAL urgency head + DETR finding boxes, trained in 3 phases (SSL → fine-tune → calibrate), served via TorchServe behind a FastAPI DICOMweb client, pulling from dcm4chee or AWS HealthImaging, writing FHIR Observations back to the RIS worklist, deployed on one A100 in Kubernetes.

Want me to go deeper on any piece — the DICOM conformance details, the CORAL loss implementation, the FHIR resource mapping, or the clinical validation study design?

# AI Triage for Radiology: Architecture, Training, and PACS Deployment

## 1. Problem Framing

"Triage" in radiology means **prioritizing and routing studies**, not diagnosis. Concretely, the system answers:

- **Urgency scoring**: Is this a 10-minute-read (massive PE, subarachnoid hemorrhage) or a 2-hour-read (routine knee)?
- **Findings flagging**: "Possible pneumothorax, right apical" surfaced to the radiologist before they open the study.
- **Routing**: Chest CT → thoracic subspecialist; lumbar spine → musculoskeletal.
- **Completeness check**: Missing views, poor contrast timing, motion artifact.

This is a **multi-task, multi-modality classification + detection** problem, not a single binary classifier.

---

## 2. Model Architecture

### 2a. Per-Modality Backbones

Don't build one monolith. Build **per-modality encoders** feeding a shared triage head.

| Modality | Backbone | Input | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chest / CT (axial) | **ViT-L/16** or **Swin-L** | 224×224 patches, 128 slices → sampled to 32–64 | Pretrained on ImageNet-22k; fine-tuned on CT |
| Chest X-ray | **EfficientNet-B4** or **ResNet-50** | 224×224, 2 views (PA + lateral) | Single-view, cheap to serve |
| MRI (brain, spine) | **3D Swin-Transformer** or **nnU-Net** encoder | 128×128×96 volumes | Use 3D convs or patchified 3D ViT |
| Mammography | **EfficientNet-B4** | 224×224, 4 views | |
| Ultrasound | **Video-Swin** or **TimeSformer** | 32-frame clips | |

**Key design choice: slice sampling for CT/MRI.** You don't feed all 500+ slices. Use a **slice-selection network** (a lightweight 1D CNN over the intensity profile of the volume) to pick the 32–64 most informative slices, then feed those to the 2D ViT. This is what Google's and Aidoc's pipelines do and it cuts inference cost ~10×.

### 2b. Shared Triage Head

```
[modality-specific encoder]
        ↓
   [CLS token / global pool]  →  768-d vector
        ↓
   [Linear 768 → 256]
   [LayerNorm → GELU]
        ↓
   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │  Task heads (all share the 256-d trunk): │
   │  • Urgency: 4-class (routine → STAT)     │
   │  • Findings: multi-label, ~50 classes    │
   │  • Routing: subspecialty classifier       │
   │  • QA flags: motion / truncation / etc.  │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Train with a **multi-task loss**: `L = λ₁·CE_urgency + λ₂·BCE_findings + λ₃·CE_routing + λ₄·BCE_qa`. Tune λ per task; findings usually dominate.

### 2c. Optional: Detection Head for Localization

For "where is the pneumothorax," add a **DETR** or **RT-DETR** head on top of the ViT backbone. Output bounding boxes + labels. This is what surfaces a visual flag on the image in the viewer.

### 2d. Ensembling / Calibration

- Train **3–5 models with different data augmentations and seeds**, ensemble at inference (average logits).
- Apply **temperature scaling** on the urgency head so the 4-class probabilities are calibrated (important for threshold-based STAT escalation).
- Keep a **per-modality, per-finding confusion matrix** in your monitoring dashboard.

---

## 3. Training Pipeline

### Data

- **Source**: De-identified DICOM from your PACS (see §4). You need DICOM *metadata* (modality, body part, laterality, acquisition protocol) as features alongside the pixels.
- **Labels**: Radiologist read reports (structured if you have C-CODes / RadLex, free-text otherwise). For free text, run a **RadNER** (radiology named-entity recognition) model — e.g., a fine-tuned BioBERT on RadLex — to extract findings. This is the single biggest bottleneck; budget real radiologist time for gold-standard labeling on a 5–10k study subset.
- **Scale**: Aim for ≥ 50k studies per modality for the encoder pretrain, ≥ 5k labeled per finding class.
- **Splits**: Split by **patient**, not by study, to avoid data leakage (same patient appears in multiple studies).

### Training Loop

```
1. Pretrain encoder on large unlabeled DICOM corpus
   (self-supervised: MAE / DINOv2 on patches, or 3D SimCLR for volumes)

2. Fine-tune encoder + triage head on labeled data
   - AdamW, lr=1e-4 (encoder) / 1e-3 (head), cosine schedule
   - Mixup + RandAugment for 2D; elastic deformation + random
     slice dropout for 3D
   - Class-balanced focal loss for findings (pneumothorax is rare)

3. Train slice-selection net jointly (end-to-end) or in a
   separate stage

4. Calibration: temperature scaling on a held-out 5% set
```

Use **PyTorch + MONAI** (for 3D transforms and DICOM I/O) or **NVIDIA Clara** if you're on DGX hardware. MONAI's `DecathlonDataset` handles DICOM → NIfTI conversion cleanly.

### Validation

- Report **per-finding AUC, sensitivity @ fixed specificity (e.g., 95% spec → what's the sensitivity?)**.
- For urgency: report **time-to-detection** in a simulated queue. "STAT cases flagged within 2 min of upload" is the metric that matters clinically.
- **External validation** on a second hospital's data before any clinical use.

---

## 4. PACS Deployment

This is where most projects die. Be specific.

### 4a. DICOM Integration

You have three integration points, and you should use **all three**:

**1. DICOMweb (the primary path)**
- Your PACS must expose **DICOMweb QIDO-RS** (query) and **WADO-RS** (retrieve). Most modern PACS (GE eNet, Siemens Syngo, Agfa IMPAX, AWS HealthImaging) support this.
- Your triage service subscribes to a **DICOMweb STOW-RS** endpoint or, better, the PACS pushes **DICOMweb transactions** to your service via a callback.
- If your PACS is older and only speaks DICOM over TCP (C-STORE), deploy a **DICOM gateway / VNA** (e.g., **Orthanc**, **dcm4chee**, or **AWS HealthImaging Archive**) that accepts C-STORE and exposes DICOMweb to your AI service.

```
Modality (CT scanner)
    │  DICOM C-STORE (TCP 104)
    ▼
  PACS / VNA  (Orthanc or dcm4chee)
    │  DICOMweb WADO-RS  (HTTPS)
    │  + HL7v2 ADT / ORM messages
    ▼
  Triage AI Service
    │  DICOMweb STOW-RS (write back AI results as
    │  DICOM SR / Secondary Capture)
    ▼
  PACS  →  Radiologist workstation (VNA viewer)
```

**2. HL7v2 / FHIR for clinical context**
- Subscribe to **HL7v2 ORM^O01** (order) and **ADT^A01/A04** (admission) messages via your integration engine (Mirth Connect / Rhapsody). This gives you patient demographics, ordering physician, clinical indication, and urgency flag from the ordering system — all features for the triage model.
- If you're on FHIR, subscribe to **Bundle** resources and **Subscription** (synchronous or webhook) for `ImagingStudy` and `DiagnosticReport` resources.

**3. DICOM SR write-back**
- When the model flags findings, write a **DICOM Structured Report** (or a **DICOM Secondary Capture** with the annotated image) back into the PACS so it appears in the radiologist's reading queue. Use **pydicom** to construct the SR with RadLex-coded findings.

### 4b. Serving Stack

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DICOMweb API (FastAPI / Flask)                        │
│  - POST /studies  (accepts DICOMweb multipart)          │
│  - GET  /studies/{uid}/triage                          │
│  - POST /studies/{uid}/sr  (write back SR)             │
└──────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┘
               │
               ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DICOM→Tensor pipeline (MONAI / dcm4chee)              │
│  - Parse DICOM, apply rescale, resample to model grid  │
│  - Slice selection for CT/MRI                          │
└──────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┘
               │
               ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Inference (Triton Inference Server or TorchServe)     │
│  - ViT-L encoder + triage head, FP16 / INT8            │
│  - Batch size 1 (studies arrive one at a time)         │
│  - Target: < 5 s per study on 1× A10G / T4            │
└──────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┘
               │
               ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Triage logic + queue management                        │
│  - Urgency score → priority queue (Redis / RabbitMQ)   │
│  - STAT → push notification to on-call radiologist     │
│  - Routing → assign to subspecialty queue              │
│  - Write DICOM SR back to PACS                         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Hardware**: A single **NVIDIA A10G (24 GB)** or **T4 (16 GB)** handles the ViT-L encoder at FP16 for one study in ~2–4 s. You don't need an A100 for triage. If you're doing 3D CT with 64 slices, budget ~8 s. Run on **Kubernetes** with a GPU node pool; autoscale on queue depth.

### 4c. Orthanc as a Practical Starting Point

If you're building this in a hospital that has a legacy PACS, **Orthanc** is the pragmatic choice:

- Open-source DICOM server, speaks DICOM C-STORE, DICOMweb, and HL7v2.
- Python plugin (`orthanc-python`) lets you hook a callback when a new study arrives.
- In the callback, pull the DICOM via the Orthanc REST API, run your model, write the SR back.
- It's not a production PACS, but as a **VNA / DICOM gateway** in front of the PACS, it's battle-tested.

### 4d. Latency & SLA

- **STAT studies** (the whole point of triage): model inference must complete within **60 seconds** of the study landing in the PACS.
- **Routine studies**: within **5 minutes**.
- Implement a **timeout fallback**: if the model hasn't returned in 90 s, the study goes to the normal queue unflagged. Never block the reading queue on AI.

---

## 5. Regulatory & Operational

- **FDA / CE**: Triage as a **decision-support** tool (not autonomous) is typically Class II (FDA 510(k)) or Class IIa (CE). You need a **clinical evaluation** with a prospective study. Start the regulatory conversation before you build, not after.
- **HIPAA / GDPR**: DICOM de-identification (PS3.15 Annex E, basic profile minimum) before data leaves the hospital. If training on-prem, keep it on-prem.
- **Model monitoring**: Track **drift** in input distributions (new scanner, new protocol) and **output drift** (urgency score distribution). Alert if the STAT rate shifts > 2σ from baseline.
- **Human-in-the-loop**: The AI flags; the radiologist decides. Log every flag and every override. This is both a regulatory requirement and your retraining data source.

---

## 6. Realistic Timeline

| Phase | Duration | Deliverable |
|---|---|---|
| Data pipeline + DICOMweb integration | 4–6 wk | Orthanc/gateway + DICOM→tensor pipeline |
| Encoder pretrain + triage head train | 6–8 wk | v0 model, internal eval |
| Radiologist labeling (5–10k studies) | 8–12 wk (parallel) | Gold-standard labels |
| Integration with PACS + queue + SR write-back | 4–6 wk | End-to-end in a shadow mode |
| Shadow mode (AI runs, humans ignore) | 4–6 wk | Sensitivity/specificity on real queue |
| Prospective clinical study + regulatory | 6–12 mo | FDA 510(k) / CE submission |

A realistic path to a **clinically deployable triage tool** is **18–24 months** from kickoff, assuming you have PACS DICOMweb support and radiologist time.

---

If you want, I can go deeper on any of these: the slice-selection network, the RadNER labeling pipeline, Triton model config for the ViT, or the Orthanc callback code. What's your current PACS stack and modality focus?

### Key architectural decisions

| Concern | Decision | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| API style | REST with versioned routes (`/api/v1/…`) | Simple, cacheable, easy to evolve |
| Auth | JWT access (15 min) + rotating refresh (7 d) stored httpOnly cookie | Stateless horizontal scaling; refresh rotation detects theft |
| ORM / query | **Knex.js** over Sequelize | SQL-first, no magic, easy to add RLS & raw perf tweaks |
| Validation | **Zod** schemas shared FE/BE | Single source of truth, runtime + TS types |
| RBAC | Middleware chain + Postgres **Row-Level Security** | Defense-in-depth: app-layer AND DB-layer enforcement |
| Bulk ops | Transactional batch with `COPY` or `UNNEST` upsert | Avoids N round-trips; atomic per batch |
| Schema mgmt (admin) | Knex migrations + a guarded `/api/v1/admin/schema` route | Admin can add/drop columns via a *whitelisted* migration runner; never raw SQL from client |
| Horizontal scale | Stateless API behind Nginx/ALB; PgBouncer in front of Postgres | Add nodes without session stickiness |

| 4.4 | `GET /admin/fields` — list all meta fields for the admin UI. |
| 4.5 | `POST /admin/users` — create a user with a specified role (admin cannot create another admin without a second-admin confirmation flag). |
| 4.6 | `DELETE /admin/users/:id` — soft-delete (set `is_active=false`); prevent self-deletion. |
| 4.7 | `GET /admin/users` — paginated user list with role filter. |
| 4.8 | Frontend: **Admin → Schema Manager** page — table of fields, "Add Field" form (name, type, nullable), "Deactivate" action. |
| 4.9 | Frontend: **Admin → User Management** page — list, create, deactivate users. |
| 4.10 | Add **audit log** middleware: log every admin mutation to an `audit_logs` table (actor, action, target, timestamp, IP). |
| 4.11 | Integration tests: admin creates field → column exists in DB; non-admin gets 403; self-delete blocked. |

**Definition of Done:** Admin can add/remove columns and manage users; all actions are audit-logged; non-admins are fully blocked.

---

### 🎫 SPRINT 5 — Security Hardening, Testing, Performance & Deployment

**Goal:** Production-grade security, comprehensive test coverage, load testing, and CI/CD deployment pipeline.

| # | Task |
|---|------|
| 5.1 | **Security audit pass**: verify `helmet` config, CORS whitelist, SQL-injection safety (parameterised queries only), XSS sanitisation on all inputs, file-upload size/type limits. |
| 5.2 | Add **CSP** headers; configure **Content-Security-Policy** in Nginx and Express. |
| 5.3 | Implement **input sanitisation** layer (`express-mysql-sanitize` or custom Zod `.transform()`). |
| 5.4 | Add **dependency scanning** to CI (`npm audit` / `snyk` / `trivy` for Docker images). |
| 5.5 | Write **E2E tests** with Playwright: register → login → CRUD → bulk upload → admin field creation. |
| 5.6 | Achieve **≥ 80 % unit + integration coverage** on `apps/api`; add coverage gate to CI. |
| 5.7 | **Load test** with `k6`: 500 concurrent users hitting `/inventory` list + bulk update; tune pool size, add DB indexes (`reference`, `name`), verify < 200 ms p95. |
| 5.8 | Implement **caching layer** (Redis) for read-heavy `/inventory` list; invalidate on write. |
| 5.9 | Configure **Nginx** reverse proxy: TLS termination (Let's Encrypt / ACM), gzip, static asset serving for React build, proxy to API. |
| 5.10 | Write **deployment runbook**: blue-green or rolling deploy via Docker Compose / ECS / Fly.io; database migration step in CI (Knex `migrate:latest`). |
| 5.11 | Set up **monitoring & alerting**: Prometheus + Grafana (or Datadog) for API latency, error rate, DB pool utilisation; Sentry for error tracking. |
| 5.12 | Final **pen-test checklist** review (OWASP Top 10); document remediations. |

**Definition of Done:** App deployed to staging; all tests green; k6 load test passes; security checklist signed off; monitoring dashboards live.

---

## 4. Key Best-Practice Principles Embedded Above

| Principle | Where it applies |
|---|---|
| **Least privilege** | RBAC middleware on every route; DB connection user has no `SUPERUSER` |
| **Defense in depth** | Helmet → Rate-limit → JWT → RBAC → Zod validation → Parameterised SQL |
| **No secrets in code** | `dotenv` + CI secrets; `.env.example` committed, `.env` never committed |
| **Reversible migrations** | Knex `up`/`down` on every migration; admin field changes are soft-delete first |
| **Stateless API** | JWT auth → horizontal scaling behind load balancer |
| **Connection pooling** | `pg-pool` (max 20) prevents DB exhaustion under load |
| **Optimistic concurrency** | `updated_at` version check on `PATCH` prevents lost updates |
| **Audit trail** | Every admin mutation logged to `audit_logs` |
| **Shared schemas** | `packages/shared` holds Zod schemas used by both API and React |
| **Containerised parity** | `docker-compose` mirrors production topology locally |

---

This plan gives you a **production-ready, role-gated inventory system** that scales horizontally (stateless API + connection pool + Redis cache) and is secured at every layer from the browser to the database. Each sprint is independently shippable, so you can demo a working system after Sprint 3 and layer admin power and hardening on top in Sprints 4–5.

# Reducing verbatim repetition loops in long-thinking models

The failure mode: during extended reasoning, the model enters a degenerate attractor and re-emits the same (or near-same) span until the token budget truncates it. Below is a brainstorm grouped by intervention point, then ranked on two axes.

## 1. Sampling

Intervene on the stochastic choice of the next token.

- **Repetition / n-gram penalty in the sampler.** The classic fix (`repetition_penalty`, `no_repeat_ngram_size`). Penalize tokens that already appeared in a recent window. Cheap, well-understood, catches exact repeats.
- **Adaptive temperature.** Keep base temperature moderate; raise it when a repetition detector fires. Avoids the quality cost of a globally high temperature.
- **Diverse / stochastic beam sampling.** Sample *k* continuations, discard any whose recent window matches the history, keep the best non-degenerate one.
- **Speculative decoding with a loop-aware verifier.** Propose cheaply, verify with the full model, and reject branches that repeat.

## 2. Decoding

Intervene on the deterministic/algorithmic path (the most direct lever for *verbatim* loops).

- **N-gram loop detection + intervention.** If the last *k* tokens reappear earlier in the sequence, truncate, restart, or inject a "conclude now" signal. This targets the exact failure mode.
- **Lookahead / backtracking.** Decode a few tokens ahead; if they form a loop, backtrack and pick the next-best branch.
- **Self-consistency / majority vote.** Decode multiple times, discard degenerate samples, vote on the answer.
- **Constrained decoding.** Forbid exact re-emission of a recent window. Effective but can degrade fluency if over-applied.
- **Early-termination heuristics.** Detect that the model has settled on an answer and stop "thinking."

## 3. Prompting

Intervene on the input side.

- **Explicit stop instruction.** "If you notice you're repeating reasoning, stop and give your answer." Low cost, but models often ignore it under long horizons.
- **Structured transition format.** Force a marker (e.g., `ANSWER:`) that signals the end of reasoning.
- **Budget-aware prompting.** Tell the model its token budget and encourage concise reasoning.
- **Few-shot good-stopping examples.** Show trajectories that conclude rather than loop.

## 4. Training

Intervene in the weights (addresses the root cause, slowest to show).

- **RL with a repetition penalty in the reward.** `reward = correctness − λ·repetition_score`. Directly optimizes against the failure.
- **DPO / preference pairs.** Prefer non-looping trajectories over looping ones on the same problem.
- **SFT on good-stopping data.** Train on concise, well-terminated reasoning.
- **Auxiliary self-similarity loss in pretraining.** Discourage n-gram self-repetition at the base-model level.

## 5. Serving

Intervene at the orchestration/infrastructure layer.

- **Chunked thinking with inter-chunk checks.** Run reasoning in segments; between segments, detect loops and restart or conclude. Robust and model-agnostic.
- **Early-stop heuristics instead of a hard cap.** Replace "stop at max tokens" with "stop when repetition is detected."
- **Production loop monitoring + fallback routing.** Detect loop patterns live; reroute to a different model version or prompt.
- **Prefix caching with a "break" continuation.** If the same prefix is produced twice, serve a cached non-looping continuation.

---

## Ranking by expected effectiveness (for verbatim loops specifically)

| Rank | Technique | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | N-gram loop detection (decoding) | Targets the exact failure mode directly |
| 2 | Repetition penalty (sampling) | Cheap, well-trodden, catches exact repeats |
| 3 | RL with repetition penalty (training) | Fixes the root cause in weights |
| 4 | Chunked orchestration (serving) | Robust, model-agnostic safety net |
| 5 | Self-consistency / majority vote (decoding) | Filters degenerate samples |
| 6 | Adaptive temperature (sampling) | Moderate; helps but indirect |
| 7 | Structured stop prompting (prompting) | Helps but often ignored under long horizons |
| 8 | SFT / DPO on stopping (training) | Real but slow to manifest |

## Ranking by cost to test (low → high)

| Rank | Technique | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Prompting changes | Trivial — edit system prompt, A/B |
| 2 | Repetition penalty (sampling) | Trivial — config flag |
| 3 | N-gram loop detection (decoding) | Low — a few lines + threshold tuning |
| 4 | Adaptive temperature | Low–medium |
| 5 | Serving-side chunking / early-stop | Medium — infra change |
| 6 | DPO / SFT on stopping | Medium–high — data + fine-tune |
| 7 | RL with repetition reward | High — GPU-weeks, reward design |
| 8 | Pretraining auxiliary loss | Very high — full pretraining run |

---

## Practical recommendation

The best **effectiveness-per-cost** moves are the three cheapest that directly hit the failure mode:

1. **N-gram loop detection in decoding** (rank 1 effectiveness, rank 3 cost) — highest leverage.
2. **Repetition penalty in sampling** (rank 2 effectiveness, rank 2 cost) — add as a second layer.
3. **Structured stop prompting** (rank 7 effectiveness, rank 1 cost) — free baseline to measure against.

Stack these three first; they're nearly free to test and together catch most verbatim loops without touching quality. Reserve **RL with a repetition penalty** for when you want a durable, weight-level fix and have the training budget. Use **serving-side chunking** as a model-agnostic safety net if you can't modify the sampler or decoder.

One caveat: repetition penalties and loop detection can occasionally truncate *legitimate* re-reasoning (a model that correctly revisits a step). Tune the window/threshold against a held-out set of good long traces so you penalize loops without penalizing genuine self-correction.
